body: Four generations are in one kitchen at half past four on a Sunday. The grandmother is at the sink doing the potatoes, because nobody else does them properly. Her daughter is laying the table and telling a story about work that nobody has asked the end of. A boy of six is under that table with a plastic dinosaur, narrating a war. The teenager is on the step by the open back door with one earbud in and one out, which is the exact posture of a person keeping an option open. The radio has been on since two. Nobody remembers putting it on, and nobody has got up to turn it off.

What is worth noticing there is not that everybody likes the music. Almost certainly nobody does, entirely. It is that nobody has got up. Liking is a low bar and easily bought. Not getting up is the hard one.

A family station is one that has to work where the listeners are sixty years apart and cannot be sent to different rooms. That is the whole brief. It sounds like a sentiment. It is a constraint, and a punishing one.

Take the word agree literally, because the usual reading of it is wrong. Four people in a kitchen do not agree on music the way a committee agrees on a budget. Nobody is polled and nobody concedes. What happens in a shared room is narrower and stranger: each person separately declines to use a veto they are perfectly free to use. The grandmother would not have chosen this song, and it does not offend her. The teenager would sooner walk into the sea than request it, and he is not embarrassed to be heard in a room with it playing. Agreement, in a house with one radio, is not a shared preference at all. It is four independent decisions not to reach for the dial, made over and over by people who want different things.
The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air now. Each holds one frequency permanently. None of them is a playlist and none of them takes requests.

Programming for a whole room costs something, and the cost is why most stations decline to do it. It is far cheaper to identify the person most likely to be holding the dial — a parent, usually, somewhere between thirty and fifty — and build the hour around what that person will not switch off. Everybody else is then handled by hope. Most family radio is aimed at the parent and endured by everybody else. That is not a family station. It is a parent station with hostages, and the hostages are generally very polite about it for a decade.

The other way to fail is worse. You can average the four of them into beige: nothing loud enough to trouble the grandmother, nothing childish enough to shame the teenager, nothing specific enough to belong to anybody. Every listener is mildly accommodated and no listener is ever addressed. A room like that does not argue about the radio, because there is nothing on it worth arguing about, and the quiet that results is not agreement. It is everybody having stopped expecting anything.

The band is arranged so that a household can learn its way about without reading anything. The ministry stations sit together, the nations hold a range of their own, the always-on formats occupy the middle, and the children have frequencies of their own rather than being tolerated as a segment. Learn roughly where things live and you can put a hand on a frequency in a busy kitchen without stopping what you are doing. That is the skill a real dial teaches, and a search box teaches the opposite one.
The alternative to a shared room is not silence. It is four rooms, and it is extremely comfortable.

Be fair to it. Four private feeds mean nobody sits through anything they dislike. The teenager gets the music that is genuinely his rather than a version of it vetted by adults. The six-year-old gets songs pitched at six, sung by people who are good at that. The grandmother is not asked to absorb a drum machine at seventy-eight, which is a real kindness. Boredom is abolished and everybody is served with an accuracy that improves monthly. What none of it can do is put something in front of a person who was not asking for it. Four people returned ever more precisely to themselves, under one roof, is four people. It is not a household.
A shared room is the only place where a family can be surprised by the same thing in the same second.

A father is driving his son to an eight o’clock kick-off on a Saturday, both of them underslept, the boy eating toast out of a piece of kitchen roll. The station is on because it is always on in that car, and neither of them has an opinion about anything before nine. A song comes up that the father would have skipped in a list — an old thing, a man and a guitar and a story about his own father — and the boy reaches over without looking, turns it up, and sings the second verse. All of it. The father did not know he knew it. Nobody taught it to him — no worship night, no conversation about faith in a car. It got into him in a kitchen, on Sundays, while he was under a table with a dinosaur.
Nobody in that car was reached by a decision. He was reached by a room, over years, while the person who put the radio on was thinking about potatoes.

There is a plain price for this and it should be said out loud. A station built for a whole room will bore every individual in it some of the time. There will be a stretch of the hour that is unmistakably for the six-year-old, and the teenager will have to survive it. Nobody gets their own thing on demand, and there are wet Tuesdays when the house would honestly rather have four feeds and a bit of peace.

That boredom is not a defect in the programme. It is the programme. Sitting through three minutes that belong to somebody else in your family is not the schedule failing to serve you; it is very nearly a definition of living with people. A house in which nobody ever waits through anybody else’s song has not solved a problem. It has dissolved one, along with the room it happened in, and the radio was the last place where taking each other into account was still being practised.

So the design problem behind a family station is not about musical taste. It is whether an hour can be built in which four people, none of whom would have chosen it, all separately decline to reach for the dial — and in which each of them gets, somewhere inside that hour, three minutes that are unmistakably theirs. Get that right and the room holds. Get it wrong in the ordinary way and you have built a parent station with hostages.
All of which is theory until the kitchen is actually noisy. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: entertaining, clean, and playable in a room with a six-year-old in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in their own tongues rather than translated into them afterwards.

If you have that kitchen, start at HM 312.10 — Island Hallelujah. It will sound like the wrong answer, and that is the point. Slack-key guitar, ukulele and island reggae; Christ lifted up in the language of the islands; unhurried, melodic, with no build and no drop and nothing in it that only works if you happen to be thirty-four. Run the vetoes and see. It is not loud enough to trouble the grandmother. It is not churchy enough to embarrass the teenager in front of whoever is at the back door. It is not pitched at six, and the boy under the table will move to it anyway. And it belongs to nobody in that room, which is exactly why nobody in that room has to defend it. A station that no one has grounds to veto will outlast four stations that one person each loves.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest the kettle, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware a household actually owns. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to the home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies households are really reaching for — which is how the next station gets built, and who it gets built for.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not audition it in the good chair with everybody told to be quiet; that is not what it is for. Put HM 312.10 on next Sunday at two, before anybody arrives, and then forget about it. Let it run through the cooking and the table and the argument about the potatoes. If nobody has got up to change it by four, you will know more about that station than a fortnight of careful listening on your own could have told you.
